## The idea

There are two natural ways to hand someone a polyhedron.

- **From the outside**, by listing inequalities: "everything with $Ax \le b$." This is
  how an LP is written.
- **From the inside**, by listing building blocks: "all averages of these corner points,
  plus any nonnegative amount of these directions."

The **Minkowski–Weyl theorem** says the two descriptions always describe the same
family of sets. Every polyhedron can be generated from finitely many points and
directions, and every set generated that way is a polyhedron.

## The math

For finite sets $V = \{v^1, \dots, v^k\}$ and $R = \{r^1, \dots, r^\ell\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$,
write
$$
\operatorname{conv}(V) + \operatorname{cone}(R)
= \Big\{ \sum_i \lambda_i v^i + \sum_j \mu_j r^j \;:\;
\lambda \ge 0,\ \textstyle\sum_i \lambda_i = 1,\ \mu \ge 0 \Big\}.
$$

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (Minkowski–Weyl)
A set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a polyhedron, $P = \{x : Ax \le b\}$, if and only if
$$
P = \operatorname{conv}(V) + \operatorname{cone}(R)
$$
for some finite sets $V$ and $R$. In particular, $P$ is a polytope (a bounded polyhedron)
if and only if it is the convex hull of finitely many points.
:::

The polytope case goes back to @minkowski1896, and @weyl1935 proved the version for
cones: a cone is generated by finitely many vectors if and only if it is defined by
finitely many linear inequalities. The decomposition of a general polyhedron into a
polytope plus a cone is usually credited to Motzkin's 1936 dissertation. See the
historical notes in @schrijver1986 for the full story.

### What $V$ and $R$ are

- The cone part is always the **recession cone** $\operatorname{rec}(P) = \{d : Ad \le 0\}$:
  the directions in which you can move forever from any point of $P$ without leaving it.
  It is $\{0\}$ exactly when $P$ is bounded.
- If $P$ is pointed (contains no line), the smallest choice of $V$ is the set of
  **vertices** of $P$, and the smallest choice of $R$ is one vector along each **extreme
  ray** of the recession cone. Nothing smaller works, and nothing else is needed.

So for a polytope, "list the vertices" and "list the facets" are two complete
descriptions of the same object.

### The two descriptions can differ wildly in size

Switching from one description to the other is always possible, but it can be
expensive.

| Polytope in $\mathbb{R}^n$ | Inequalities | Vertices |
|---|---|---|
| Cube $\{x : 0 \le x_j \le 1\}$ | $2n$ | $2^n$ |
| Cross-polytope $\{x : \sum_j \lvert x_j \rvert \le 1\}$ | $2^n$ | $2n$ |

For $n = 30$, the cube has 60 inequalities and over a billion vertices. This asymmetry is
why algorithms are built around one representation or the other, and never convert
blindly.

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: inequalities ⇒ points and directions
Take $P = \{x : Ax \le b\}$, pointed for simplicity. Let $V$ be its vertices and $R$ the
extreme rays of $\{d : Ad \le 0\}$; both are finite. Clearly
$\operatorname{conv}(V) + \operatorname{cone}(R) \subseteq P$.

For the reverse, take $x \in P$ and argue by induction on the dimension of the smallest
face containing $x$. If $x$ is a vertex, we are done. Otherwise pick a direction $d$
inside that face. Moving along $d$ and $-d$, at least one way hits a new constraint
(there is no line). If both do, $x$ lies on a segment between two points of
lower-dimensional faces; if only one does, $x$ is a point of a lower-dimensional face
plus a recession direction. Either way the induction hypothesis applies.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: points and directions ⇒ inequalities
The set $Q = \operatorname{conv}(V) + \operatorname{cone}(R)$ is the projection onto
$x$ of the polyhedron
$$
\{(x, \lambda, \mu) : x = \textstyle\sum_i \lambda_i v^i + \sum_j \mu_j r^j,\
\lambda \ge 0,\ \sum_i \lambda_i = 1,\ \mu \ge 0\}.
$$
A projection of a polyhedron is again a polyhedron: eliminate the extra variables one at
a time, combining inequalities pairwise (Fourier–Motzkin elimination). Each step keeps a
finite list of linear inequalities, so $Q$ has one too.

A cleaner route uses duality: apply the first half of the theorem to the *polar* of
$Q$, and translate back with a separation argument.
:::

## In practice

- **LP and IP formulations are inequality descriptions.** Solvers never list vertices.
- **Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition uses the inner description.** Each subproblem polytope
  is replaced by "a convex combination of its vertices," and column generation produces
  those vertices on demand. See
  [Dantzig–Wolfe: Theory and Mechanism](../../decomposition-methods/dantzig-wolfe/theory-and-mechanism.qmd).
- **Projections stay polyhedral.** That is why extended formulations work: describe a
  set with extra variables, and its projection is still a polyhedron. The hull
  formulation in [Big-M vs. the Convex Hull](../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/big-m-vs-hull.qmd)
  is an example.
- **Unboundedness has a certificate.** If an LP is unbounded, there is a ray $r$ of the
  recession cone with $c^\top r > 0$ (for maximization).
